How the package is checked

Source: vignettes/articles/simFastBOIN-validation.Rmd
simFastBOIN-validation.Rmd

Four kinds of checks

Every design of the package is checked in four ways.

  • Tests. The test suite in tests/testthat/ checks every function on cases whose results are known: decision tables printed in the articles, limiting cases in which a design reduces to a simpler one with the same random numbers, and values computed beforehand by a separate implementation.
  • Separate implementations. The trials of every simulation engine were compared, trial by trial, with an implementation of the same rules written in Python and fed with the random numbers of R, whose default generator was written again in Python for that purpose. These implementations are development files and are not part of the package.
  • Reference implementations. The scripts in inst/validation/ compare the package with other R packages and with the code of the authors of a design, exactly where the rules and the random numbers are the same and within simulation error otherwise.
  • Published results. The scripts in inst/reproduce/ compare the package with the tables and figures of the articles that introduced the designs.

This article summarizes the last two. The scripts write their judgments to the results/ folders of inst/reproduce/ and inst/validation/, and every number below is read from those files.

Judgments

Every compared value receives one of four judgments.

  • PASS. The value agrees: exactly, or to the printed digits, for a value that involves no random numbers, and within the tolerance stated in the script for a simulated value. Where the package and the reference draw the same trials, the values must be equal; otherwise the tolerance is a number of standard errors of the difference between two independent simulations, three or four as the script states, plus the rounding of the printed value.
  • EXPLAINED. The value lies outside the tolerance for a reason that was found, such as a misprint in the article, or a rule of the program of the authors that the article does not describe. The reason is registered in inst/validation/explained.csv, which has 399 rows.
  • FAIL. The value lies outside the tolerance and no reason was found. These values are kept and listed below.
  • INFO. The value is listed for information and not judged: for example the results of the default rules of the package where an article used other rules, or a quantity that an article does not describe well enough to be compared.

A script is run from the root of the source package after devtools::load_all(). It defines its functions, and the function named in the usage at the top of the script runs the comparison and writes the results file, for example

devtools::load_all()
source("inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2021.R")
res <- run_reproduce_zhou2021()
table(res$design, res$judgement)

Some scripts take a long time, up to a few hours, and those that compare with other packages need these packages.

Of the 11,456 values judged by the 22 scripts, 10,930 pass, 399 are explained and 127 fail, and 4,146 more are listed for information. The sections below describe what each script compares.

Designs that select the MTD

iBOIN. reproduce_Zhou2021.R compares iboin_boundary() with the boundaries of Table 1 of Zhou et al. (2021), exactly, and the simulations with the rows BOIN, iBOIN and iBOINR (the robust prior) of Table S.1 of its supporting information, five operating characteristics in ten scenarios, within four standard errors plus 0.05. The article does not say whether its simulations select the MTD with or without the prior information; they are judged with it, and the selection from the data alone is INFO.

BOIN, TITE-BOIN, BF-BOIN and BE-BOIN. compare-with-BOIN.R compares sim_boin() with BOIN::get.oc() over a grid of configurations, by equality, since the two draw the same trials for the same seed, and compare-with-Zhao2024.R compares BF-BOIN with Table 4 of Zhao et al. (2024). These scripts print their results and do not keep a results file in the package; the tests check the agreement with the ‘BOIN’ package on smaller settings. The decision tables of TITE-BOIN are reproduced by the tests entry by entry.

The BOIN-ET family

BOIN-ET and TITE-BOIN-ET. reproduce_Takeda2018.R compares the boundaries and the decision tables of Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2018), exactly, and the operating characteristics of Table 3, within four standard errors plus 0.5 for the rounding. reproduce_Takeda2020.R does the same for Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2020), whose simulations did not wait for finished assessments (min_completed_share = 0). compare-with-boinet.R compares sim_boin_et() and sim_tite_boin_et() with boinet_compatible = TRUE with boinet::boinet() and boinet::tite.boinet(), within four standard errors plus 0.05.

Of the values that fail, listed at the end of this article, 10 of the 14 of Takeda et al. (2018) and 17 of the 29 of Takeda et al. (2020) are in scenario 11, whose printed response rate of 0.55 at the lowest dose does not fit the published results; the ‘boinet’ package too selects that dose far more often than the article reports. In Takeda et al. (2020) the early terminations, durations and allocations of TITE-BOIN-ET in scenarios 8, 9, 10 and 12 agree better with an exclusion of doses that uses only the patients whose outcomes are known, which the article does not state. The other values that fail are not explained.

gBOIN-ET. reproduce_Takeda2022.R compares the boundaries printed in Takeda et al. (2022) and Table 1. The SAS program of the authors draws one Bernoulli variate for every category and takes the highest that comes up, so that the categories are not drawn with the probabilities of Table S1; the judged rows simulate the probabilities that the program draws, with the printed boundaries, the linear fractional polynomial, min_obd_sample = 6, independent outcomes and boinet_compatible = TRUE, within four standard errors plus half a unit of the printed digit. The rows with the probabilities of Table S1 and with the default rules are INFO. compare-with-gboinet.R compares sim_gboin_et() with boinet::gboinet() under four selection rules, within four standard errors plus 0.05.

TITE-gBOIN-ET. reproduce_Takeda2023.R compares the boundaries printed in Takeda et al. (2023) and Table 1 and Tables S2 to S6. The R program of its supporting information, written again in C++ with the random numbers of R, reproduces the summaries that the supporting information holds for the program exactly. It differs from the article and from ‘boinet’ in two points: where one dose has the highest mean efficacy score among the current dose and its neighbors, it passes that dose to sample(), which then draws from all doses up to it, and it excludes doses with the effective numbers of patients. The published cells are judged with the rules of ‘boinet’, and those that these two points move out of the tolerance are explained; the same simulations are also judged against the program without the two points. compare-with-tite-gboinet.R compares sim_tite_gboin_et() with boinet::tite.gboinet(), within four standard errors plus 0.05.

U-BOIN. There is no reference implementation. reproduce_Zhou2019.R compares the boundaries of Table 2 and Table S2 of Zhou, Lee and Yuan (2019), the utility tables S4 to S6 of its supporting information and the true utilities, to the printed digits, and the simulations of Table 3 and Tables S8 and S9, within four standard errors plus half a unit of the printed digit, with the rates of Scenario 7 of Table S8 for Scenario 7 of Table 3 and with s1 = 12 for Table S8, with which the published results agree. The admissibility of Tables S4 to S6 is judged with the default prior and with prior_resp = c(0.05, 0.05), which reproduces it, and the simulations with the printed rates and with the s1 = 9 of the text are judged as well.

compare-with-BOINETC.R 1 The mean numbers of patients of this row of Table S5 add up to 26.21, whereas #N of Table S1 is 26.1 for the same trials; with the values of the code at A2B1 (7.66) and A2B2 (3.04) they add up to 26.10. A translation of the code of the authors into Python, fed with the random numbers of R after set.seed(1234), gives 7.656 at A2B1 and every other value of the run to the printed digits except A2B2.
compare-with-BOINETC.R 1 The row of Table S6 (17.8 / 58.3 / 18.0) appears shifted: 17.8 is the #N of the same scenario with BOIN-ETC2 and n_stop = 6 (Table 3), whereas the code of the authors gives a %ODC of 81.4 for these trials and this utility, and its %ODC for the other two utilities agrees with Tables 3 and S7 (81.4 and 90.8).
compare-with-BOINETC.R 1 The row of Table S6 (80.3 / 59.6 / 26.1) takes 80.3 and 26.1 from Table S1 (n_stop = 9, utility 100-40-60-0) for the same scenario and design. The code of the authors gives a %ODC of 78.7 for these trials and this utility, and its %ODC for the other two utilities agrees with Tables 3 and S7.
compare-with-BOINETC.R 1 The row of Table S8 (60.3 / 58.3 / 26.4) appears shifted: 60.3 is the %nODC of these trials (Tables S1 and S9), whereas the code of the authors gives a %ODC of 79.3 for these trials and this utility, and its %ODC for the other two utilities agrees with Tables S1 and S9.
reproduce_Takeda2022.R 2 The SAS program of the authors sorts the 36 fractional polynomials by the first value of the fit table of PROC GENMOD, the deviance, in descending order and takes the first, the model with the largest deviance; the article and the package take the best-fitting model. A transcription of the program in Python gives about 5.6 for dose 2 and 13.2 for dose 6 with the largest deviance, within the allowance (published 4 and 14), and about 6.2 and 10.7 with the smallest, as the package (about 6.5 and 10.3)
reproduce_Takeda2022.R 1 The difference is at the edge of the allowance (about 2.5 against a published 1, allowance about 1.5). A transcription of the SAS program of the authors in Python gives about 1.9 (10,000 trials), within the allowance. The program differs from the package in the points listed in inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2022.R (no posterior probability rules during the trial or at the selection, the fractional polynomial with the largest deviance); which of them accounts for this cell was not isolated
reproduce_Takeda2022.R 1 The SAS program of the authors has no posterior probability rules. It ends a trial at the lowest dose when the design would stay or de-escalate there and the mean efficacy score is at most half the target or the toxicity score reaches a count boundary, and it recommends no dose when no dose up to the MTD has six patients; the package ends a trial when the posterior probability rules of the article exclude every dose, which happens less often here (about 0.6 against a published 2). A transcription of the program in Python gives about 1.7 (10,000 trials), within the allowance
reproduce_Takeda2023.R 297 The program of the supporting information of the article passes the dose with the highest mean efficacy score to sample(), which draws from all doses up to it when it is a single dose, and excludes doses with the effective numbers of patients; neither is in the article or in boinet::tite.gboinet(). A transcription of the program reproduces all its published summaries exactly, and with these two points removed it gives the value of the package within simulation error (row ‘TITE-gBOIN-ET against the corrected program’)
reproduce_Lin2020.R 1 Six patients with two DLTs and three responses give 0.191. The same row of Table S.3 reports a response rate of 0.50 for dose 4, whose three patients had no response, so the row appears to hold a misprint
compare-with-escalation.R 6 Doses 1 and 2 have low response rates and become inadmissible. The rules of ‘escalation’ (admissibility of the neighbouring doses only, de-escalation to the dose below whatever its data, end of the trial when no neighbouring dose is admissible, OBD selected without the admissibility check) were written again in Python and give the values of ‘escalation’ within simulation error, and the rules of simFastBOIN written in Python give those of sim_boin12() (8000 trials each; Scenario 2: DL1 20.8 and 14.8, DL3 19.1 and 27.3, no OBD 13.0 and 4.7; Scenario 4: no OBD 1.3 and 0.4)
reproduce_Zhou2022.R 3 Table 2 gives 0.118 when a pending outcome is replaced by pi_hat and 0.117 by Equation (11), with pi_hat = (0.43, 0.44). The table reports pi_hat = (0.37, 0.55), but at day 315 two responses are observed and two patients have completed the response window without response at dose 3, so that pi_E is at most 0.50 whatever the convention; the row was computed from data other than Table 2
reproduce_Zhou2022.R 1 The three patients at dose 4 had no response, so pi_E is 0. The value 0.56 repeats that of dose 3, as in the BOIN12 row of the same analysis, and appears to be a misprint
reproduce_Zhou2019.R 16 The supporting information gives s1 = 9 for Table S8, but its U-BOIN-CD rows agree with s1 = 12, which the rows of the design U-BOIN use.
reproduce_Zhou2019.R 12 Tables S4 to S6 mark a dose without any response inadmissible, which the efficacy prior Beta(0.05, 0.05) reproduces (rows U-BOIN, efficacy prior Beta(0.05, 0.05)). The simulations of the article agree with the default Beta(1, 1) prior, under which these counts are admissible.
reproduce_Zhou2019.R 7 The results of Scenario 7 of Table 3 agree with the rates of Scenario 7 of Table S8 (DLT 0.03, 0.08, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55; efficacy 0.05, 0.25, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45), not with the rates printed in Table 3; the rows of the design U-BOIN use the rates of Table S8.
reproduce_Zhou2019.R 1 The article prints 0.358, the value common in the BOIN literature; lambda_d for the target 0.30 is 0.35852, which rounds to 0.359.
